issues.legal_issue: The applicable town-planning procedure did not require individual service of a special notice on every person affected by the scheme.
material_facts: A public notice was issued during the proceedings for preparation and finalisation of the scheme.
The tenant objected to the draft scheme but did not pursue that objection and filed no objection to the re-allotment proceedings.
The governing procedural rule provided for publication of notice and an opportunity for affected persons to submit objections; it did not prescribe individual service of special notice.
issues.conclusion: The applicable rule did not mandate individual special notice. The Court also declined to examine in these proceedings whether the rule was invalid for failing to require such notice, since that challenge had not been raised.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 52 and 81 of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, and Rules 26(1) and 26(3) of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Rules, 1979, provide for notice and participation in the scheme process but do not contemplate individual service of special notice. The Court distinguished the earlier decisions in Mansukhlal Jadavji Darji v. Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation and Jaswantsingh Mathurasingh v. Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, which concerned Rule 21 of the Bombay Town Planning Rules, including its requirement for special notice; the relevant rule had since been amended and was not the rule applicable here.

predicates.town_planning_scheme_proceeding: The authority conducted proceedings to prepare and finalise a town-planning scheme affecting land occupied by the person.
predicates.general_notice_published: The authority published a general notice about the scheme proceedings.
predicates.affected_person_had_opportunity_to_objec: The affected person had an opportunity to inspect or respond to the scheme proposals.

issues.definition: When a town-planning authority publishes general notice and gives affected persons an opportunity to object, individual special notice is not required under a procedure that does not prescribe it.

issues.legal_issue: A person who knowingly fails to pursue an objection or claim during scheme proceedings and allows the scheme to become final may waive a notice-related right and lose the ability to obtain equitable public-law relief against the completed scheme.
material_facts: The tenant knew of the scheme and initially objected to the draft, but did not pursue that objection.
Despite public notice, the tenant did not object to or participate in the proceedings for re-allotment or claim compensation or continued possession of the remaining land.
The scheme and final allotments became final, including an allotment to another owner that incorporated the disputed land.
The Court assumed, without deciding, that the tenant was entitled to special notice and treated the notice benefit as one intended for the tenant, with no public interest involved.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming a right to special notice existed, the tenant waived that right by his conduct and could not obtain equitable relief reopening the final scheme or asserting an interest in the allotted land in the public-law proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: A right provided for an individual's benefit, where no public interest is involved, may be waived expressly or by conduct; waiver requires awareness of the relevant facts and the right, and may be inferred where conduct is inconsistent with continuing to assert it. The Court relied on Manak Lal v. Dr. Prem Chand, Director of Inspection of Income Tax v. Pooran Mal & Sons, Krishna Bahadur v. Purna Theatre, Bank of India v. O.P. Swarnakar, and Ramdev Food Products Pvt. Ltd. v. Arvindbhai Rambhai Patel. It also applied the principle that a party may be denied equitable relief after allowing matters to reach an irreversible stage.

rule.if: public_law_challenge_to_finalized_town_planning_scheme and claimant_knew_of_claim_opportunity and claimant_abandoned_objection_or_claim and scheme_reached_finality

predicates.public_law_challenge_to_finalized_town_p: The person brought a public-law challenge concerning a town-planning scheme that had been finalised.
predicates.claimant_knew_of_claim_opportunity: The claimant knew of the scheme proceedings and had an opportunity to assert an interest or objection.
predicates.claimant_abandoned_objection_or_claim: The claimant began but did not pursue an objection, or failed to make a claim during the relevant later proceedings.
predicates.scheme_reached_finality: The scheme and resulting allotments became final before the claimant sought relief.

issues.definition: Where a claimant knew of an opportunity to assert a claim, abandoned it, and challenged the scheme only after it became final, the claimant may be treated as having waived the notice-related right and barred from equitable public-law relief.

issues.legal_issue: Final allotment under a town-planning scheme does not determine the private rights between a landlord and tenant, and a tenant who has no enforceable claim against the authority may pursue an appropriate claim against the landlord.
material_facts: The tenant occupied part of land owned by the landlord, while the final plot was allotted to the landlord and the disputed remaining land was included in a plot allotted to another owner.
The tenant did not raise a claim for allotment, compensation, or continued possession during the scheme proceedings.
The dispute over the tenant's entitlement concerned the distribution of benefits between private parties rather than unjust enrichment by the State.

The Court held that the tenant had no enforceable claim against the State at that stage but could pursue an appropriate proceeding against the landlord, with the State or authorities joined if appropriate.
issues.conclusion: The tenant could not obtain relief against the State or reopen the final allotment on this record, but remained at liberty to pursue an appropriate claim against the landlord concerning their inter se rights or compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 67 and 82 of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, address vesting of land and compensation, while Section 81 concerns transfer or extinction of rights. The Court distinguished vesting for the authority's purposes from re-allotment as part of town planning, which distributes benefits in pursuit of the scheme. It relied on State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas for the principle that town planning may confer development benefits on owners, and on the statutory procedure discussed in Maneklal Chhotalal v. M.G. Makwana. The scheme does not, merely by making a final allotment, resolve private inter se claims between landlord and tenant.

predicates.public_law_challenge_to_completed_town_p: The tenant challenged the authority's implementation of a town-planning scheme after its allotments were completed.
predicates.private_landlord_tenant_entitlement_disp: The asserted entitlement concerned the division of property or compensation between a landlord and a tenant.
predicates.tenant_did_not_raise_claim_during_scheme: The tenant did not seek allotment, compensation, or continued possession during the scheme proceedings.

issues.definition: When a tenant brings a public-law challenge after completing a scheme but did not raise a private entitlement claim during it, the tenant cannot obtain relief against the authority on that basis but may pursue the private claim against the landlord.
